1.pericope_label: He cried also in mine ears with a loud voice, saying, Cause them that have charge over the city to draw near, even every man with his destroying weapon in his hand. And, behold, six men came from the way of the higher gate, which lieth toward the north, and every man a slaughter weapon in his hand; and one man among them was clothed with linen, with a writer’s inkhorn by his side: and they went in, and stood beside the brasen altar. And the glory of the God of Israel was gone up from the cherub, whereupon he was, to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed with linen, which had the writer’s inkhorn by his side; And the Lord said unto him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering punishments of the city, which does not suit a context that introduces the men who execute them, and render the mark a cross. Ellicott denies the six can be earthly officers, since the phrase every man is used constantly of angels; he makes the man in linen a seventh, refuses to identify him either with the Babylonian god of writing or with Christ, endorses the cross-shaped letter on the evidence of the old script and the coins, and insists the marking regards character alone.

Gill hears the loud voice as calling the ministers of vengeance together, reports the rabbinic identification of the six with named enemy generals, and takes the movement of the glory as proof that a divine Person is meant. Calvin reads the opening phrase as a command rather than a noun of visitation, finds the Chaldeans indicated by the northern gate, and says outright that he has not discovered why the number is six, dismissing the attempt to derive it from a list of enemy leaders elsewhere.

Clarke takes the six for the Chaldeans and the party for an eastern monarch's seven counsellors, the man with the inkhorn keeping the book of death and the book of life; on the mark he knows the whole cross tradition and rejects it for this place, since the Hebrew says only that a mark shall be made and the vision binds us to no figure. Wesley leaves the six open, preferring angels, and gives each his own instrument.

Henry keeps the reading the others reject and plays on it, the visitors of the city being at hand for a people who would not know their day of visitation in mercy; he subordinates the Chaldean armies to the angels as mere tools, counts one destroyer for each principal gate, and compares Sodom, which had two where this city has six.

debates.question: Who are the six men with the slaughter weapons?

positions.position: Angelic executioners, not earthly officers; the phrase every man is used constantly of angels.
The Chaldeans, the north gate being the direct way from Babylon.
Left open: either angels or the named enemy generals.

debates.question: What does the number six signify?

positions.position: One for each principal gate; Sodom had two destroying angels where this city has six.
Nothing discoverable; the derivation from a list of enemy leaders elsewhere is varying and forced, and God may only have meant to show a small band sufficient.
Six with the man in linen makes a seventh, completing a mystical number.

debates.question: Is the mark on the foreheads a cross?

positions.position: Yes: the word is the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script and on the coins had the form of a cross.

The tradition is known and rejected for this place: the Hebrew says only that a mark shall be made, the thing functions as the blood on the doorposts did, and a vision binds us to no letter or figure.

outliers.claim: Refuses both current identifications of the man in linen, with the Babylonian god of writing and with Christ, on the ground that nothing in the text gives the figure any identity: he is an angelic messenger sent to mark the faithful, and no more.
Reads the whole party as the seven counsellors of an eastern monarch, the man with the inkhorn being the minister who kept the book of death and the book of life.

5.pericope_label: And to the others he said in mine hearing, Go ye after him through the city, and smite: let not your eye spare, neither have ye pity: Slay utterly old and young, both maids, and little children, and women: but come not near any man upon whom is the mark; and begin at my sanctuary. Then they began at the ancient men which were before the house. And he said unto them, Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain: go ye forth. And they went forth, and slew in the city.

schools.summary: Ellicott allows no interval between the marking and the slaughter, judgment waiting only until those mercy will spare are secured; he takes the passage for one of many in which God is revealed as taking vengeance at last without pity, and explains that the defilement of the house, the touch of the dead being the utmost pollution the older economy knew, is itself part of the judgment rather than an obstacle to it.

Gill makes the order to defile an instruction not to hesitate, since those who defiled the house with abominations may now defile it with their blood. Calvin dismisses the whole cross-mark tradition as puerile and nugatory, draws from the marking instead the doctrine that God never lays aside the care of his own, and meets the objection that the house was polluted already by distinguishing the pollution the people would have recognised from the one they walked past every day.

Clarke makes beginning at the sanctuary a rule of proportion, those who sinned against the most mercy and privilege being the first victims and the unfaithful within the church punished most, while warning anyone outside not to enjoy the spectacle; on the order to defile he hears a dreadful sentence, the house given over because God will dwell in it no longer.

Henry presses the absence of exception, neither the beauty of the virgins nor the innocency of the babes securing them, and warns that sparing whom God has doomed is doing God's work deceitfully; he explains the beginning at the sanctuary causally, the debaucheries of the priests having poisoned the springs, and alone concludes that the slaughter in the house was a purification of it rather than a pollution.

debates.question: Is the mark to be understood as a letter or a cross?

positions.position: Neither: the word means simply a mark; the derivation from the word for the law is puerile and the report of a Samaritan cross a figment.
By proportion: those who sinned against the most mercy and privilege are punished first and most.
By cause: the wickedness began there, the priests' debaucheries poisoning the springs to which the corruption of the streams was owing.
Because the gross sin of the people had culminated there, and the destruction was to be utter.

debates.question: What does defiling the house amount to?

positions.position: A sentence of abandonment: the house is given to pollution because God will dwell in it no longer.
Part of the judgment itself, justice overriding the technicalities of defilement.
An instruction not to hesitate: those who defiled it with abominations may now defile it with their blood.
Ceremonially a pollution, but in reality a purification, since it put away evil.

outliers.claim: Offers in jest a better puzzle than the ones he has dismissed: if the faithful must be marked with the last letter of the alphabet, let it be because they are last among men.

Answers the objection that the house was polluted already by distinguishing two pollutions: a corpse or a dog in the sanctuary they would have cried out upon as portentous, while they walked in themselves loaded with blood, rapine and perjury and counted that nothing.

8.pericope_label: And it came to pass, while they were slaying them, and I was left, that I fell upon my face, and cried, and said, Ah Lord God! wilt thou destroy all the residue of Israel in thy pouring out of thy fury upon Jerusalem? Then said he unto me, The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceeding great, and the land is full of blood, and the city full of perverseness: for they say, The Lord hath forsaken the earth, and the Lord seeth not. And as for me also, mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity, but I will recompense their way upon their head. And, behold, the man clothed with linen, which had the inkhorn by his side, reported the matter, saying, I have done as thou hast commanded me.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the form behind I was left as an incongruous fusion of participle and imperfect and plainly a copyist's slip, reading it as a participle rather than emending it. Ellicott gives the scene instead of the form, the courts lately thronged with idolaters now a city of the dead with the prophet alone in it, hears only sternness in the reply, and explains the closing report as the sign that those marked for mercy are not forgotten.

Gill grounds the sentence in what the people did rather than what they said, and notes a Syriac reading that turns the last verse into a sight rather than a fact. Calvin takes the disputed form as meaningful rather than corrupt, answers the objection that not everybody was killed by observing that the survivors were as good as dead, and reads the divine answer as restraining the prophet's fervour while asserting the equity of the judgment.

Clarke names the dead the prophet had just watched fall, gives the forsaking saying its narrower sense of this land and explains why God resents it, answers the claim that he does not see with the eye that has seen everything and will neither pity nor spare, and turns the closing report into a general rule that angels and men alike must account personally for what they have done.

debates.question: How should the form behind I was left be treated?

positions.position: As a copyist's error, an incongruous fusion of participle and imperfect, to be read as a participle rather than emended.
As meaningful: the word looks compounded of two tenses or of two persons, and the sense is unambiguous whatever the grammar.
The words simply imply left alone, in a city of the dead.

debates.question: What is the ground of the sentence?

positions.position: The saying that the Lord has forsaken this land, which reduces him to an idol or a provincial deity.
What they did rather than what they said: not sparing the poor, the widow and the fatherless, perverting judgment and shedding innocent blood.

debates.question: Why is the closing report included?

positions.position: To show that those marked for mercy, though too few to affect the impression of the vision, are not forgotten.
As a rule that angels and men alike must account personally for what they have done, and as news that the penitents are all signed and safe.
As a direction to call to mind the distinguishing goodness of God towards his own, the Syriac reading it as a sight.

outliers.claim: Answers the objection that not everybody was in fact killed: the slaughter nearly destroyed the name of the people, the survivors were as good as dead since exile was worse to them than dying, and the vision carries the threat out to the last penalty that waits on the ungodly.

Reads the prophet's complaint as suppliant rather than contentious, which is why an answer capable of calming him is given, and generalises that other prophets who take similar liberties return directly to themselves.
